title: Numbers and age
goal: Count to a million, ask and give your age with the verb *ter*, and say phone numbers like a Brazilian — including their habit of swapping the number six for another word.
bekal: count 0-100 and build big numbers with *e*
use *ter* for age — "have twenty-five years", not "be twenty-five"
ask about prices and numbers with *quanto* and *qual*

notes: **Age is something you have, not something you are.** *Eu tenho vinte e cinco anos* literally means "I have twenty-five years". Translating straight from English as *eu sou vinte e cinco* is a mistake people hear immediately — and the easiest one to avoid, since there's only one pattern.

**⚠️ Meia, not seis.** A Brazilian habit textbooks rarely teach. When reading out phone numbers or addresses, Brazilians replace *seis* (six) with **meia** — short for *meia dúzia*, "half a dozen". The reason is practical: *seis* and *três* sound too alike over the phone. If you hear *meia* in a string of digits, it means **six**, not half.

**Phone numbers are read digit by digit.** *Nove seis dois* is said one by one, not combined into "nine hundred sixty-two". The first two digits are the area code — 11 for São Paulo, 21 for Rio de Janeiro.

**Tem also means "there is".** *Quantos alunos tem na turma?* is literally "how many students does it have in the class?", but it means "how many students are there". In Brazil, *tem* expresses existence just like "there is/are": *Tem café?* = "Is there any coffee?", *Não tem problema* = "No problem". The formal form *há* exists too, but lives almost only in writing.

**Anotei** is a past form — "I've noted it down". It's not time to learn it yet; for now just recognize that the ending **-ei** marks something that has already happened. The whole past tense chapter is waiting in unit 15.

grammars.title: Ter — "to have", the most versatile verb
body: After *ser* and *estar*, this is the third verb you must learn whole. It's used for possession, age, existence, and — later in unit 12 — obligation.
after: ⚠️ *tem* and *têm* **sound exactly the same**. The little hat on *ê* is only a spelling mark to tell singular from plural; your ears can't hear it, and Brazilians often get it wrong in writing too.
Four jobs of *ter* to recognize now: *Eu tenho um carro* (possession), *Eu tenho vinte anos* (age), *Tem café?* (existence), and *Tem que estudar* (obligation — unit 12).

grammars.title: Numbers 0 to 20
body: Twenty-one words to learn whole. After that, you can build the rest yourself.
after: ⚠️ **One and two have feminine forms.** *Um livro* but *uma mesa*; *dois livros* but *duas mesas*. No other number changes at all. This mistake tends to linger because it seems trivial — yet *duas horas* and *dois anos* come up in conversation every day.
Notice that 16 to 19 are built from *dez* + the digit: *dez-e-sseis*, *dez-e-ssete*, *dez-oito*, *dez-e-nove*. After 20, every number is built with the word **e** ("and") in the middle.

grammars.title: Numbers 20 to a million
body: From here on, everything can be built. There's only one rule: put **e** between the parts.
after: ⚠️ **Cem becomes cento as soon as another number follows.** Exactly one hundred = *cem*; 101 and up = *cento e um*, *cento e vinte*. It's the only number that behaves this way.
**Hundreds have feminine forms**: *duzentos reais* but *duzentas pessoas*; *quinhentos livros* but *quinhentas casas*. Same rule as *um/uma* and *dois/duas*.
⚠️ In Brazil, **dots and commas are swapped** compared with English: *1.000* means one thousand, and *3,5* means three point five. You'll see it on every price tag.

blocks.text: Two question words cover nearly every number question: *quanto* (how much/how many) and *qual* (which; what, for numbers).

⚠️ *Quanto* changes to match its noun: *quantos anos* (masculine plural), *quantas pessoas* (feminine plural), *quanto dinheiro* (masculine singular). *Qual* doesn't change except in the plural: *quais*.

Look at the fifth row: Portuguese asks *qual é* ("which is") for phone numbers and names, not *o que é*. Saying *o que é o seu nome* is a mistake that instantly marks a foreigner — even though English uses "what".
Brazil's currency is the **real**, plural **reais** (said heh-EYES). The symbol is R$, written before the number: R$ 25,00.
In everyday conversation the cents part is shortened: R$ 10,50 is simply *dez e cinquenta* — just like saying "ten fifty" in English without naming the currency.
